methodological_rigor.justification: Very small single-center retrospective cohort (n=26; POD12 n=12, no-POD12 n=14) with targeted 103-gene NGS panel. Design is descriptive and hypothesis-generating; no multivariable survival modeling adjusting for IPI or other prognostic factors, no multiplicity correction across many gene-level and pathway-level tests, and no validation cohort. Follow-up is short (median 23 months). Confidence intervals for several hazard ratios (HR 12.13, 95% CI 2.34-62.78) are extremely wide, reflecting severe sample-size limitation. Key comparisons rely on chi-square/Fisher's exact for single genes, t-tests for response comparisons where a chi-square is more appropriate.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Small retrospective cohort/case series with biomarker correlation maps to Oxford LoE 4. POD12 in DLBCL is clinically important; identifying biomarkers predicting early failure has translational value, but findings here are exploratory and not generalizable. Clinical utility is unclear given small sample and absence of validation.

reporting_quality.justification: Biomarker/prognostic study; REMARK checklist applies. Reporting addresses patient characteristics, sample source, and sequencing pipeline (tools, versions, thresholds) but omits many REMARK items: no prespecified hypothesis/statistical plan, no sample-size justification, no adjustment for established prognostic factors (IPI), no internal/external validation, no handling of multiplicity, and inconsistent labeling (e.g., 'CARID1A' likely means 'ARID1A'; 'CD78B' typo in figure legend). No raw sequencing data accession number, no code availability, and no REMARK checklist reference.

novelty_literature.justification: Re-examines known DLBCL mutation landscape (KMT2D, CD79B, TP53, MYD88, CREBBP, EP300) and their relation to POD12 - an extension rather than discovery. The specific finding that CD79B wild-type associates with POD12 is interesting but runs counter to some prior literature; several cited studies (Reddy 2017; Schmitz 2018; Wright 2020; Chapuy 2018; Dubois 2016) have already explored genomic predictors in DLBCL, including with much larger cohorts. Contribution is incremental and hypothesis-generating.

writing_presentation.justification: Manuscript has multiple grammatical and typographical errors ('JACK-STAT' instead of 'JAK-STAT', 'CARID1A' for 'ARID1A', 'CD78B' in figure 3B legend, 'Progressive-free survival' instead of 'progression-free', 'POD12 subtype was mostly characterized by mutations in the epigenetic modulation pathway (33.32%)... whereas the no-POD12 subtype is mostly characterized by mutations in the epigenetic modulation pathway (40.66%)' which reports the same pathway for both groups without clear contrast). Structure follows IMRaD but several sentences are awkward or inverted. The abstract's opening sentence is grammatically broken.

key_strengths: Addresses a clinically important problem (POD12) in DLBCL with integrated NGS and interim response data
Identifies two candidate markers (CD79B wild-type status and lack of interim CR) with internally consistent statistical associations
Clear NGS pipeline reporting (BWA-MEM, VarScan2, ANNOVAR, IGV) facilitates replication of the bioinformatic workflow
key_concerns: Very small sample (n=26) with extremely wide HR confidence intervals (e.g., HR 12.13, 95% CI 2.34-62.78) and no validation cohort
No multivariable adjustment for IPI or Hans COO; no multiplicity correction across many gene-level tests
Multiple nomenclature/typographical errors (CARID1A, CD78B, JACK-STAT) and a contradictory pathway description (epigenetic modulation listed as dominant in both groups)
Biomarker-study reporting does not meet REMARK expectations (no prespecification, no validation, limited confounder handling)
No data availability statement or sequencing-data accession; limits reproducibility
Finding that CD79B wild-type predicts POD12 conflicts with parts of prior literature and needs validation
chief_reviewer.rationale: Exploratory, underpowered NGS correlation study with notable reporting and nomenclature issues; suitable only for a Tier 4 hematology/oncology journal and only after major revisions to clarify statistical rigor, add validation, and correct errors.
